extracted.intended_audience: military officers, Judge Advocate/ Judge Advocate General's Corps, court-martial members, and military legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive synopsis of the Articles of War giving definitional rules, jurisdictional limits, prosecutorial/doctrinal criteria, and illustrative holdings used to apply and enforce the Articles in courts-martial and military administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on Army bands receiving remuneration / competing with civilians
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of May 11, 1908 (35 Stat. 110) forbids Army bands or members thereof receiving remuneration for furnishing music outside the limits of military posts in competition with local civilian musicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holds that a musician on the retired list who is not a band or member thereof does not come within the inhibition. Volunteer bands composed of enlisted men maintained at posts may fall within the prohibition. Purchasing instruments or expending public money for bands not authorized by law is not authorized; Secretary of War procurement is restricted to reasonable needs of legally authorized bands, but use of accumulated excess instruments may be permitted to promote enlisted men's welfare. (C.24179; C.23870 and cited rulings.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditure for unauthorized bands not authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenditure of public money to furnish music for bands that are not authorized by law as part of the military establishment is not authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive lacks authority, unaided by legislation, to establish bands in the military service. Secretary of War restricted in procurement to reasonable needs of law-authorized bands. Where surplus instruments exist, Secretary may permit their use to promote welfare, comfort, and contentment of enlisted men. (C.23870.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Volunteer bands status and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Volunteer bands at military posts are not organizations established by law as part of the Army; their treatment differs from legally authorized bands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not legally part of the Army, volunteer bands composed of enlisted men maintained at posts may be treated as within the prohibition against competing with civilian musicians; procurements for them are limited to reasonable needs of authorized bands, with exceptions when surplus instruments can be used for welfare. (C.23870; C.16739.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey order first, question legality afterwards
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier receives an order of doubtful legality, it is his duty to obey it and seek redress afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the soldier disobeys in the first instance, his action is an offense (generally under Article 62). This rule is stated as 'Obey Order First, Question Legality Afterwards.' (See Article XXI D.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 21 — 'Willful refusal or neglect' (disobedience) defined
rubrics_metrics.description: The offence of disobedience under Article 21 consists in a willful refusal or neglect to comply with a specific order to do or not to do a particular thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere failure to perform a routine duty should be charged under Article 62. Examples held to violate Article 21 include refusal to pay a debt to a company tailor or refusal, when properly detailed, to cook for a mess of civilian teamsters who are part of the command. Conversely, refusal to act as an officer's servant, refusal to contract marriage when ordered, or refusal to sign a certificate when facts are not within the officer's knowledge have been held not to violate Article 21 in certain rulings. (Rulings cited: R.33, 280; P.33,22; R.27,520; R.4,9.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of punishable acts under Article 17 ('his clothing') and relation to surveys
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'his clothing' refers to articles regularly issued to the soldier for use in service and which he may not dispose of while in service; only certain wrongful dispositions (selling, through neglect losing, spoiling) are made punishable by this article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article is independent of Army Regulations relating to surveys; surveying officer determines pecuniary responsibility while court-martial imposes punishment. Other wrongful dispositions should be charged under Article 60 or Article 62. (XVII A–C; cited rulings.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 61 — 'Conduct unbecoming' defined and exemplified
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct must be manifestly unbecoming an officer and gentleman; it is sufficient that it be morally wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances include false official statement, preferring false accusation, corruptly influencing an officer's vote, appropriating government property for personal use, officer drunk in public, disorderly fighting, gambling in public with enlisted men, bigamy, abusing wife, manufacture of false testimony, duplication of pay accounts, continued dishonorable nonpayment of debt, etc. (LXI A–B and listed examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 54 — Liability for damage to person or property; assessment and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 54 includes damage to person or property and makes action mandatory; assessment may be upon the whole command with exceptions and may be in addition to punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure and applicability vary (men in regular army vs militia); assessment enforceable in certain overseas jurisdictions (e.g., Cuba and Philippines) but may not be enforceable in favor of military persons in some cases (e.g., embezzlement). General court-martial cannot be used instead of required boards in some situations. (LIV A–H.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 62 — Definition of 'crimes' and catalogue of offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 62 defines 'crimes' and lists a wide range of offenses (improper publication of criticism of an officer, unauthorized withdrawal/payment of public funds, failure to account for public money, offenses against civilians, offenses against nature, burglary, larceny, false swearing, improper disposition of property, disrespectful language, disobedience of NCO order, drunkenness, loaning at usurious rates, disturbance on private premises, delays in return, failure to obey orders, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article also sets out instances of disorders or neglect, acts which are not offenses under Article 62, and addresses manslaughter under its provisions. Many specific rulings flesh out proper charging and scope. (LXII A–F and related pages.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent jurisdiction with civil authorities and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction of military courts may be concurrent with civil authorities in many offenses; sentences sometimes must be equal to or greater than state law provisions when jurisdiction is concurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local laws of a foreign country do not apply in some contexts; limitations and specific applications (e.g., in Philippines during military occupation) are discussed. (LVm A–C and related discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may convene courts-martial and convening authority powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Convening authorities (e.g., department, division, separate brigade commanders) have authority to order courts-martial and to decide on number of members; certain officers cannot convene or add/relieve members; powers depend on command status and rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules include limits when requisite number of members not at post, who may serve as members or judge advocates on various courts (regular vs volunteers), and that convening authority decisions are final on organization. (Articles 72–79 and LXXII–LXXVIII commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules on deposits/depositions and evidence (use and admissibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions must be submitted as a whole; they may not be excluded by the court; depositions of high public officers should be taken by deposition and there are limitations (e.g., not to be read in capital cases in some contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositions taken abroad, reasons for not receiving depositions, authority of court over deposition, and interaction with Sixth Amendment concerns are discussed. (LXXX–LXXXV commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Double jeopardy / no person tried twice for same offence
rubrics_metrics.description: No person shall be tried twice for the same offense; 'jeopardy' means conviction or acquittal without regard to action of reviewing authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstances when reconsideration is not a second trial, relation to prior courts of inquiry, and examples (one act but two offenses) are discussed. (Article 102 and related pages.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of time for prosecution and procedural continuances
rubrics_metrics.description: There are statutory limitations on time of prosecution and recognized good grounds for continuance (e.g., to procure counsel, copy of charges materially differs from original).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules on limitation statutes, continuance grounds, and their application (e.g., in capital cases) are explained. (Articles 103; XCm commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval, confirmation, and review of sentences (including death sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences require approval or confirmation by the officer ordering the court or higher authorities; death sentences and certain dismissals require additional confirmations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles 104–111 set out processes for approval, confirmation of death sentences, confirmation by officer ordering court, and which authorities may act; considerations in fixing sentence and consulting statutes are noted. (Articles 104–111 and CVI–CVII commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pardon and mitigation: authority and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to pardon and to mitigate sentences is defined; the power to pardon cannot be delegated and does not include authority to commute or substitute in many cases; mitigation is defined and illegal sentences or dishonorable discharges cannot be mitigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power of mitigation of sentence of inferior courts resides in the actual commanding officer; illegal sentences cannot be mitigated; certain limitations continue after approval. (Articles CXII–CXIII commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts of inquiry — nature, use, and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of inquiry is a board and not a demandable right; its opinion is confined to special questions; a minority report is permitted; proceedings may be used to impeach witnesses and may be used as evidence in later proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts of inquiry have specified members, oaths, witness rules, authentication, and limits on opinion scope. Proceedings forwarded to Judge Advocate General and rules on copying and use are described. (Articles 115–121 and CXV commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of critical terms ('infamous criminal offense', 'on post', 'on duty', 'enemy')
rubrics_metrics.description: Key statutory/interpretive definitions used in construing the Articles: 'infamous criminal offense' means punishable by penitentiary imprisonment or death; 'on post' and 'on duty' are defined; 'enemy' and other terms are defined for jurisdictional and charging purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions determine application of many articles (e.g., whether capital sentences have been imposed in wartime, when statutes run for desertion). Examples and case citations clarify borderline applications. (Various article commentaries: III A; 'On Post' defined; 'On Duty' defined; 'Enemy' defined.)
